articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'Film for Television - Alive or Dead' (Digest No.115)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Film for Television - Alive or Dead
IEE Colloquium on Film for Television - Alive or Dead
abstract: Both film material and telecines for the conversion from film to TV have been continuously improved during the last decade. Novel CCD telecine technology and experience gained from the development of an experimental CCD telecine for HDTV permits now sizing and repositioning by the use of an EDTV CCD scanner and a full resolution sizing principle.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Perspective from the facility company (film for TV)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Film for Television - Alive or Dead
abstract: Examines the changes in the methods of video post production. SVC Television built one of the first off-line editing suites. They also found the need to build a cross-fire type telecine to transfer from film to U-matic, the rushes for the edit. It has been suggested that the video camera gave superior quality and therefore would supercede film before the end of the 1980s. However, commercials are still being shot on 35 mm film. That film would be used to transfer cutting copies to U-matic video tape.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Film for Television - Alive or Dead
abstract: The main stream film production for theatrical release and TV commercials concentrates on four perforation 35 mm and TV productions use both this format and 16 mm, with Super 16 mm recently entering the field of play. The size of images and their attendant resolutions, film density range and density discrimination, and the benefits of originating on film for both todays and future TV production are examined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Perspective from the broadcaster (film for TV)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Film for Television - Alive or Dead
abstract: Discusses the advantages and disadvantages of using film for TV production. A film camera can be more tolerant of rough handling and extreme climatic conditions than a video one. It also has a colour viewfinder that could be used all day without running down the batteries. Film is however more vulnerable than videotape. It must be handled with care to avoid dirt and scratching. Telecines are essential, and very expensive, requiring highly skilled individuals to operate and maintain them.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Film for Television - Alive or Dead
abstract: The prospect of high definition video could revitalise existing and well established media giving them a new exciting life. HD video has much to offer in both the areas of acquisition and post production. The Electron Beam Recorder (EBR) was developed by Sony to provide high quality transfer of electronic images from HDVS tape to 35 mm film. The main advantages of the EBR are extremely fine and sharp image, no halation, excellent colour reproduction, and good archiving.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Film for Television - Alive or Dead
abstract: Independent Television Facilities Centre (ITFC) has the responsibility for all acquired material owned by the Independent Television Network. The Centre is responsible for some 50000 titles, comprising over 30000 separate items. Many of the items were badly scratched, and all needed cleaning. For cleaning the film a cold fluid process was chosen. The machines in use provide good wind tension and allow new reels to be spliced on without replacing, thus minimising handling and maximising throughput. By transferring the film stocks to videotape, the film can be retained as archive material. New film purchases are transferred to D2 tape format using telecines.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Film and high resolution electronic systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Film for Television - Alive or Dead
abstract: Outlines the reasons why film's role will intensify, and Kodak's work to add another dimension to the situation. That is the development of advanced systems based on scanners, laser writers, optics and digital processing. Systems that exploit the best combinations of film and video technology. The new generation of EXR motion picture films and a CCD HDTV telecine were developed to support film origination in the era of HDTV. The telecine was designed to translate film's superior image quality to any of the proposed HDTV standards. Another development is the high resolution digital image manipulation system for motion picture film, called the High Resolution Electronic Intermediate System.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Film for Television - Alive or Dead
abstract: Video, having no sprocket holes or edge numbers, utilises an electronic means of numbering the frames called time code. A continuous, frame by frame count which is used in all areas of production and post production, and has enabled various tasks to be automated. Time code principles are applied to film originated material for use with 'off-line' edits, and consequent film confirmation, either to produce an 'on-line' edited transfer, or indeed to cut the original negative.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Film for the cinema and film for TV-is there a difference?
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Film for Television - Alive or Dead
abstract: It is in considering future distribution requirements that the universal standard of film master material has a high value today. HDTV systems rivalling 35 mm film are being developed, primarily for electronic post production and special effects at the present time. However, 35 mm film remains the highest quality universal medium for both television and the cinema. The purpose of this paper is to highlight and discuss those factors which make film such a flexible medium for meeting the present and future needs of TV and the cinema. Image quality, aspect ratio, telecine transfer, post production, and the existing film libraries are examined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
